The Weekly Gleaner launched with a blitz of 36 agents in 1857 then rapidly disappeared; The Israelite built steadily to a peak of 59 agents in 1861; The Messenger grew sharply to 38 in 1859. Agent tenure data is available for agents with start and end years recorded.

Do a paper’s subscribers actually relate to where its agents were? Three independent tests. The first two find a strong spatial association; the third asks whether it is causal — and finds it is not.

1. Town-level correlation (Spearman’s ρ)

Rank correlation between the number of a paper’s agents in a town and the number of its subscribers there. 0 = none, 1 = perfect. All four are positive and statistically significant (p < 0.001).

2. Subscribers clustered near agents (within 25 mi)

Share of each paper’s subscribers living within 25 miles of one of its agents (solid) versus what random agent placement would produce (faded). The gap is the clustering effect.

3. Did subscriptions rise after an agent arrived? (causal test)

For every town that gained an agent on a known date, we compare the town’s share of its paper in the 3 years before vs. the 3 years after — which controls for the paper’s overall growth. If agents created subscribers, most towns should rise.

How to read this together: subscribers cluster around agents far more than chance (tests 1–2), but towns were no more likely to gain share after an agent arrived than to lose it (test 3). The most defensible conclusion is that agents were appointed where Jewish reading communities already existed, rather than generating new subscribers. Correlation is strong; causation is not supported by these data. Caveats: only The Israelite has enough dated agent-towns for the causal test; agents whose appointments coincided with a paper’s launch have no “before” window; record survival varies by year.
